purpose: Close nine selected v153 mock-coverage application gaps using original Year 1 theoretical questions

limits.provenance: Original revision examples aligned to AQA content, not official mark schemes

questions.subject: Physics
questions.prompt: A velocity–time graph has three straight segments: (i) from t=0 to 4.0 s, velocity is +6.0 m s⁻¹; (ii) from 4.0 to 7.0 s it falls linearly from +6.0 to −3.0 m s⁻¹; (iii) from 7.0 to 9.0 s it remains at −3.0 m s⁻¹. Calculate net displacement and total distance; identify the direction of motion from 7.0 to 9.0 s.
markPoints: First interval displacement is +6.0 × 4.0 = +24 m.
On the second interval, v=0 at t=6.0 s.
Second-interval positive area is ½ × 2.0 × 6.0 = +6.0 m.
Second-interval negative area is ½ × 1.0 × 3.0 = −1.5 m.
Third interval displacement is −3.0 × 2.0 = −6.0 m.
Total displacement is 24 + 6 − 1.5 − 6 = +22.5 m.
Total distance is 24 + 6 + 1.5 + 6 = 37.5 m; last interval is negative-direction travel.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.prompt: On an unfamiliar curved displacement–time graph, a tangent at t=3.0 s passes through two clearly read points (1.0 s, 4.0 m) and (5.0 s, 20.0 m). Determine the instantaneous velocity at t=3.0 s, state its direction and explain why using a tangent is appropriate rather than finding the gradient of the whole curve.
markPoints: A tangent to the displacement–time curve is used at the specified instant.
Change in displacement along tangent is 20.0 − 4.0 = 16.0 m.
Change in time is 5.0 − 1.0 = 4.0 s.
Tangent gradient = 16.0/4.0 = +4.0 m s⁻¹.
Positive gradient indicates motion in the positive direction.
The tangent gives instantaneous velocity whereas a chord over a time interval gives average velocity.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.subtopic: Horizontal projectile launched from a raised platform
questions.prompt: A ball leaves a raised platform horizontally at 16.0 m s⁻¹ and lands 45.0 m below its launch point. Ignore air resistance, and use g=9.81 m s⁻². Calculate time of flight, horizontal distance, vertical component of impact velocity and magnitude of impact velocity. Explain why horizontal and vertical components share the same flight time.
markPoints: Horizontal acceleration is zero; horizontal velocity stays 16.0 m s⁻¹.
Vertically, displacement −45.0 m = ½(−9.81)t², giving t = √(90.0/9.81) = 3.03 s.
Horizontal distance = 16.0 × 3.03 = 48.5 m.
Vertical impact velocity = −gt = −29.7 m s⁻¹.
Impact speed = √(16.0² + 29.7²) = 33.7 m s⁻¹ approximately.
Horizontal and vertical motion occur simultaneously, so the same elapsed time is used.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.subtopic: Area and stiffness from a piecewise-linear force–extension plot
questions.prompt: A force–extension graph joins (extension 0.000 m, force 0 N), (0.040 m, 80 N) and (0.080 m, 110 N) using straight line segments. Determine the initial stiffness, the work done to extend to 0.040 m and to 0.080 m, and explain why extrapolating the first segment's stiffness to 0.080 m is inappropriate.
markPoints: Initial stiffness is the initial force–extension gradient.
Area from 0 to 0.040 m is ½ × 80 × 0.040 = 1.60 J.
Total work done to 0.080 m is 1.60 + 3.80 = 5.40 J.
The second segment has a different gradient so stiffness is not constant across the full range.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.subtopic: Experimental V–I graph with lost volts
questions.prompt: Measurements for a cell give terminal p.d. V=1.60 V at I=0 A, V=1.40 V at I=0.50 A and V=1.20 V at I=1.00 A. Treat the graph V against I as a straight line. Determine emf, internal resistance, lost volts and terminal p.d. at 1.00 A; explain the meaning of the negative graph gradient.
markPoints: The V-axis intercept at zero current gives emf ε = 1.60 V.
The internal resistance is r = 0.40 Ω, the magnitude of the negative gradient.
Lost volts at 1.00 A are Ir = 1.00 × 0.40 = 0.40 V.
Terminal p.d. at 1.00 A is ε − Ir = 1.20 V.
The negative gradient shows increasing current causes greater internal voltage drop and hence smaller terminal p.d.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.subtopic: Finite load changes a potential divider output
questions.prompt: A 12.0 V ideal supply is connected to a potential divider with a 2.0 kΩ upper resistor and a 4.0 kΩ lower resistor. Output is measured across the lower resistor. A 4.0 kΩ load is then connected in parallel with the lower resistor. Calculate the unloaded output, loaded effective lower resistance and loaded output. Explain the change.
markPoints: The load is parallel with the lower 4.0 kΩ resistor.
The effective lower resistance is 1/(1/4.0 + 1/4.0) = 2.0 kΩ.
The output falls by 2.0 V.
With a smaller lower-branch resistance, a smaller fraction of the 12.0 V supply appears across it.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: Two liquids, straight-chain hexane and 2,2-dimethylbutane, both have formula C₆H₁₄. Hexane has the higher boiling point. Explain why, referring to structure and intermolecular forces. Explain why a claim that hexane has more electrons is incorrect.
markPoints: The two substances have the same molecular formula, C₆H₁₄.
They therefore have the same total number of electrons per molecule.
Hexane has a less branched, more extended molecular shape.
Its molecules can generally achieve greater contact surface area with neighbours.
This tends to strengthen induced dipole–dipole (London/van der Waals') forces and increase hexane's boiling point.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: Use the supplied mean bond enthalpies (kJ mol⁻¹): C=C 612; C–C 347; C–H 413; H–H 436. For the conceptual reaction C₂H₄ + H₂ → C₂H₆, estimate ΔH using bonds broken minus bonds formed. Explain why a result using mean bond enthalpies is approximate.
markPoints: One C=C bond and one H–H bond are broken in the net change.
Energy for bonds broken = 612 + 436 = 1048 kJ mol⁻¹.
One C–C bond and two additional C–H bonds form.
Energy released by bonds formed = 347 + 2(413) = 1173 kJ mol⁻¹.
Mean bond enthalpies are average gaseous-bond values and are approximate for particular molecules.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.subtopic: Correct a calorimetry cooling curve by extrapolation
questions.prompt: In an illustrative calorimetry data exercise, mixing occurs at t=60 s. The original mixture temperature is 20.0 °C; after the reaction, the cooling-line readings are 38.0 °C at 120 s and 36.6 °C at 180 s. Treat cooling as linear over this interval. Find the corrected maximum temperature at t=60 s and calculate ΔH when 50.0 g solution (c=4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹) absorbed heat from 0.100 mol of reaction. Explain why extrapolation is used.
markPoints: Extrapolation backwards 60 s to mixing time gives corrected maximum = 38.0 + 1.4 = 39.4 °C.
Corrected temperature rise = 39.4 − 20.0 = 19.4 K.
Heat gained by solution q=mcΔT = 50.0 × 4.18 × 19.4 = 4054.6 J.
Convert q to 4.0546 kJ.
Extrapolation compensates for heat exchange with surroundings before the maximum can be measured directly.
